title: Evidence for a low-gap component in compressively stressed niobium thin films
authors: J. T. Paustian, Maciej Olszewski, Kiichi Okubo, Lingda Kong, B. L. T. Plourde, Ethan G. Arnault, Caleb W. Fink, Valla Fatemi, Ivan V. Pechenezhskiy
abstract: We investigate the microwave response of sputtered Nb films as a function of biaxial film stress. Although transport measurements show nearly identical superconducting transition temperatures ($9.0\pm 0.2$K) and residual resistance ratios across the stress series, microwave resonators fabricated from highly compressive films exhibit enhanced temperature-dependent loss and larger frequency shifts. A conventional single-phase Mattis--Bardeen description yields an effective critical temperature of $2.4\pm0.2$K, approximately a factor of four below the value obtained from transport measurements. We show that the data are instead consistent with the presence of an additional low-gap component whose contribution increases with compressive stress. These results show that conventional transport measurements can overlook stress-dependent low-energy excitations that strongly influence microwave performance.
summary: This study investigates how intrinsic biaxial stress affects the superconducting properties of niobium thin films by comparing DC transport measurements with high-precision microwave resonator measurements. The authors find that while DC measurements suggest a stable superconducting state, the microwave response reveals a strong, stress-dependent loss mechanism. They conclude this anomalous behavior is due to a secondary, low-gap superconducting component, demonstrating that microwave techniques are necessary to detect subtle, stress-induced low-energy excitations.
main_problem: The study investigates the discrepancy between superconducting properties measured by DC transport versus microwave response in niobium thin films, particularly focusing on the influence of intrinsic biaxial film stress.
main_result: The anomalous microwave response, characterized by enhanced loss and frequency shifts in highly compressive films, is attributed to an additional, stress-dependent low-gap superconducting component, which is missed by conventional transport measurements.
method: The research uses microwave resonators (CPW) to measure loss and frequency shifts across varying film stresses, complementing DC transport measurements and employing two-component superconducting models for fitting.
model_or_system: The system is niobium (Nb) thin films sputtered under controlled biaxial stress. The analysis uses a two-component model to fit the microwave response, separating the contribution of the main superconducting phase from a secondary, low-gap component.
key_observables: Microwave loss (1/Q_i), relative frequency shift (Δf/f), superconducting transition temperature (Tc), and residual resistance ratio (RRR).
important_parameters: Biaxial in-plane stress (up to 1 GPa), low-gap critical temperature (Tc_2nd ≈ 2.4 K), and cryogenic temperatures (down to 70 mK).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the Mattis–Bardeen basis functions are valid approximations and that the anomalous response is dominated by the secondary component, ruling out vortex motion as the primary cause of the thermal loss.
figures_summary: Figures show the stability of transport properties (Tc, RRR) versus stress, contrasted with the strong stress dependence of microwave loss and frequency shift. Later figures confirm the fit to a two-component model and rule out vortex contributions by comparing zero-field and field-cooled measurements.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the discrepancy between transport and microwave measurements under stress. It then develops a two-component model to fit the microwave data, identifying the low-gap component. Finally, it rigorously tests alternative sources of anomalous loss, such as trapped vortices, and rules them out.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum optics because it demonstrates how subtle, low-energy excitations (the low-gap component) can dominate macroscopic measurements (microwave response) even when the primary superconducting gap remains robust, providing a model for hidden degrees of freedom in condensed matter.
